question: The pain in acute appendicitis classically begins as central/periumbilical colicky pain before migrating to the right iliac fossa. Which mechanism explains this migration?

answers.text: The appendix moves from the central abdomen to the right iliac fossa as inflammation progresses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The appendix does not move — it is fixed in (or near) the right iliac fossa. The migration of pain reflects a change in the type of pain, not the position of the organ.

answers.text: Initial visceral pain (midgut T10 dermatome, felt centrally) is replaced by somatic parietal pain as inflammation reaches the peritoneum overlying the appendix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Distension of the appendix stimulates visceral afferents (T10, referred centrally). As transmural inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic afferents from the right iliac fossa take over — producing the characteristic migration. This two-phase pain is one of the best discriminators for appendicitis.

answers.text: Referred pain from right-sided ovarian pathology initially felt centrally then lateralising

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ovarian pathology does not explain the sequence in this classic appendicitis scenario. The mechanism is visceral-to-somatic pain transition driven by the spread of inflammation to the parietal peritoneum.

overallFeedback.feedback: The migratory pain in appendicitis is explained by visceral (central, poorly localised) pain from appendicular distension being replaced by somatic (sharp, localised) parietal peritoneal pain as inflammation extends to the overlying peritoneum.
Correct. Central visceral pain (T10) → peritoneal involvement → right iliac fossa somatic pain. This migration is one of the most specific clinical features of appendicitis.
